title: Preparing to Build the House of the LORD
summary: Hiram, king of Tyre and a longtime friend of David, sends envoys to the new king, and Solomon replies with a plan to build a house for the Name of the LORD, as God promised David. Hiram agrees to supply cedar and cypress from Lebanon, floated by sea, in exchange for yearly shipments of wheat and olive oil, and the two kings make a treaty. Solomon conscripts a large labor force from Israel and sets thousands of porters and stonecutters to quarry great stones for the temple's foundation.
story: The whole story of David's house has been moving toward this. David wanted to build a house for God, and God answered through Nathan that David's son would build it, while God would build David a house, a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:5-13). Solomon now quotes that promise and begins to act on it. His explanation of why David couldn't build (constant wars) complements the reason given in 1 Chronicles 22:8, that David had shed much blood. The phrase rest on every side echoes Deuteronomy 12:10-11, which promised that when God gave Israel rest from its enemies, he would choose a place for his name to dwell. The conditions for the temple are met. The chapter also shows the cost of building: a treaty with a foreign king and a conscripted workforce drawn from Israel itself.
historical:
Tyre was the leading city of the Phoenicians, a seafaring people on the coast of what is now Lebanon, famous for trade, shipbuilding, and craftsmanship. Hiram of Tyre is also known outside the Bible: the first-century Jewish historian Josephus reports that Tyrian records, cited by earlier writers, mentioned Hiram and his dealings with Solomon. Lebanon's mountains held great forests of cedar, prized throughout the ancient Near East for temples and palaces; Egyptian and Mesopotamian kings also boasted of obtaining cedar from Lebanon. The Sidonians (a general term for Phoenicians here) were renowned for their skill in cutting and moving it. The Gebalites of verse 18 were men of Gebal, the Phoenician city the Greeks called Byblos.

The timber was brought down to the coast, tied into rafts, and floated south along the shore; 2 Chronicles 2:16 names the port as Joppa, from which it was carried up to Jerusalem. The payment of wheat and olive oil reflects the complementary economies of the two kingdoms: Phoenicia's narrow coastland had timber and trade but little farmland, while Israel had grain and olives. In the Hebrew Bible this chapter begins at what English Bibles call 5:1 but is numbered 5:15, because the Hebrew counts the end of chapter 4 as the start of chapter 5.
cultural:
Building a temple was the supreme act of an ancient Near Eastern king. Royal inscriptions regularly record that a god gave the king rest from enemies and then the king built or restored the god's house, often with timber from Lebanon. Solomon's project fits that pattern, but with a distinctive theology: the temple is a house for the Name of the LORD. In Deuteronomy, God's Name dwelling in a place expresses his real presence and ownership while protecting his transcendence; the God of heaven cannot be contained in a building (1 Kings 8:27).

Forced labor (the corvée) was a common institution in the ancient world. Subjects owed the king a certain amount of labor each year on public works. Solomon's rotation, one month in Lebanon and two at home, softened the burden, but the numbers were huge. First Kings 9:20-22 says that Solomon made the remaining Canaanite peoples into permanent slave labor and did not enslave Israelites, while 5:13-14 describes a labor levy drawn from all Israel. Many interpreters distinguish between permanent slavery for Canaanites and temporary conscripted service for Israelites. Either way, the resentment over this burden is what the northern tribes voice in chapter 12.
literary: The chapter is built around an exchange of diplomatic messages between two kings, a genre familiar from ancient royal correspondence. Solomon's message (verses 3-6) moves from theology to business: God's rest, God's promise, and then the practical request for cedar. Hiram's reply (verses 7-9) begins with praise of the LORD and moves to terms of trade. Verse 12 is the hinge, joining the two things the chapter wants the reader to see together: the LORD gave Solomon wisdom as he promised, and there was peace and a treaty with Hiram. The chapter then turns to the labor force with a series of large numbers, stressing the scale of the undertaking and the weight it placed on the people.

outline.t: Solomon asks Hiram for timber to build the temple
Hiram's agreement and the treaty between the kings
The labor force, stonecutters, and foundation stones

doctrines.note: Solomon builds because God promised David that his son would build a house for God's Name. The temple is the fulfillment of a covenant promise, not simply a royal vanity project.
God's gift of rest from enemies makes the temple possible, and even a pagan king praises the LORD for giving David a wise son. God's purposes move forward through international politics and trade.
The temple is for God's Name, a way of speaking of his real presence among his people while insisting that he is greater than any building. The idea shapes the whole temple section of 1 Kings.

words.note: Banah, to build. It appears six times as the chapter prepares for construction. In 2 Samuel 7 the verb carried a play on words: David's son would build a house for God, and God would build a house (a dynasty) for David. Both kinds of building are in view as the temple begins.

Shem, name. The temple is repeatedly called a house for the Name of the LORD. In the Bible a name expresses identity and reputation, and God's Name in the temple means God himself present and known there, without being confined to the building.

Satan, adversary. Solomon says there is no adversary (verse 4). The word usually means simply an opponent, human or heavenly; only later does it become the proper name of the devil. Ironically, God will raise up adversaries, using this very word, against Solomon in 11:14 and 11:23 after his heart turns away.

Mas, forced labor or a labor gang. It names the system of conscripted work Solomon uses for his building projects. The word marks the cost behind the temple and palaces, and it anticipates the complaint that splits the kingdom in chapter 12.

christ: The temple Solomon prepares to build is the house where God places his Name among his people, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the fulfillment of what the temple meant. John writes that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), using a word that recalls the tabernacle. Jesus spoke of the temple of his body (John 2:19-21), and the apostles describe the church as a spiritual house built of living stones (1 Peter 2:5) and a temple in which God dwells by his Spirit (Ephesians 2:21-22). Solomon's great stones, quarried at great cost to lay the foundation, stand behind the New Testament's language of Christ as the cornerstone. The contrast is as important as the link: Solomon's house was built with forced labor, while the church is built by a king who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). These are thematic connections drawn by the New Testament, not predictions within the chapter.
questions: Solomon waited for rest before building. What does it look like to build something for God out of peace rather than out of anxiety or pressure?
The temple required the labor of tens of thousands of people. Whose unseen work lies behind the worship and ministry you benefit from?
Hiram, a foreign king, praised the LORD for Solomon. How can faithful work and fair dealing lead outsiders to recognize God?
